senses: A hermit crab.
ety: From hermit + -ie.
examples: Your hermies need a second home to chill out in whenever they're sick or molting.

senses: To make quiet or put at rest; to pacify or appease; to quell; to calm.
To alleviate; to abate; to mitigate.
ety: From Middle English alayen, aleyen, aleggen, from Old English āleċġan (“to put, place, lay down, lay aside, throw down, give up, cease from, abandon; put down, allay, suppress, abolish, conquer, destroy, overcome, refute; lay upon, inflict, impose upon; diminish, take away, refuse, lessen, withhold”), from Proto-Germanic *uzlagjaną (“to lay down”), equivalent to a- + lay. Cognate with German erlegen (“to impose, cause to succumb, kill”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌻𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (uslagjan, “to lay down”). In Middle English the word was identical to forms of allege and alloy, leading to much overlapping of senses.
examples: They were forced to try to allay discontent by palliative measures.
He had to pretend to be drunk in order to allay the suspicions which might have been aroused by his appearance at the gate.
Kissinger was obviously doing his best to allay our government's growing apprehension in connection with Nixon's forthcoming trip to Peking.

senses: A person who has epilepsy.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπιληπτικός (epilēptikós).
examples: The present Immigration Act on the books bars entry to Canada to homosexuals, prostitutes, epileptics, and those said to be "living off the avails of homosexualism or prostitution."

senses: Of, related to, or abounding in palm trees.
Prosperous, flourishing, booming or thriving.
ety: From palm + -y.
examples: So, all things being equal, from the beginning of my stay with Travis, I was in as palmy and benign a state as I could remember in many years.

senses: A child's game, in which a player, hopping on one foot, drives a stone from one compartment to another of a figure traced or scotched on the ground.
ety: From hop + scotch (“scratch”).
examples: No-one. Meade’s timberyard. Piled balks. Ruins and tenements. With careful tread he passed over a hopscotch court with its forgotten pickeystone.

senses: To instruct or improve morally or intellectually.
ety: From Old French edifier (“to build, to edify”), from Latin aedificare (“build”).
examples: That they ought to edify one another by maintaining and promoting the knowledge of truth.

senses: A Central and Eastern European coffee cake flavored with orange rind, rum, almonds, and raisins; or with some single flavoring, such as chocolate or lemon.
ety: From a Slavic language likely via Yiddish באַבקע (babke). Compare baba (“rum soaked cake”).
examples: These festive, fudgy confections are a mash-up of two traditional Jewish favorites: rugelach and chocolate babka.
And while you’re there, you can pick up a babka, which you’ve heard about (a twisted, sweet chocolate loaf) and a bag of rugelach which you might not have (crescent-shaped chocolate pastries).
A couple of weeks ago, my family and I also travelled an hour or so to sample the babkas and honey croissants at Farro bakery in Bristol.

senses: Of a person or thing: to take on (a different form); to adopt, to assume.
Followed by with: to invest (someone or something) with a certain power, quality, etc.
ety: From both of the following: * Chiefly sense 1: Late Middle English induen (“to clothe (someone); to assume or take on (an appearance)”), from Latin induere, the present active infinitive of induō (“to put on (clothes, etc.); to assume (a part)”), from indu- (an archaic variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in; within’)) + *uō (“to put on (clothes, etc.)”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ew- (“to put clothes or shoes on”)). * Chiefly sense 3 and sense 4: Late Middle English endeuen, enduen (“to endow; to induct or put (someone into office, etc.); (falconry) of a hawk: to pass food from the cr
examples: My transport of the afternoon, and the matter of physical contrast, made me endue the tactile apparatus of another man, any man but me, and imagine the beauty of Zip in his caressing arms.
A being whom I myself had formed, and endued with life, had met me at midnight among the precipices of an inaccessible mountain.
But after dissension / Had ended, in France, and you were endued / With your former privilege, how did you show your gratitude?

senses: A severe and rapid systemic allergic reaction to an allergen, causing a constriction of the trachea, preventing breathing; anaphylactic shock.
ety: Borrowed from French anaphylaxie, coined by French physiologist and parapsychologist Charles Richet and French zoologist Paul Portier from the Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “(intensifier) thoroughly”) from ᾰ̓νᾰ́ (ănắ, “to, again, upon”) and φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “protection, watching, guarding”).
examples: He said a bite could send someone into anaphylaxis, which is a narrowing of the airways and lowering of blood pressure, within minutes.

senses: The name of the Latin script letter H/h.
ety: From Middle English ache, borrowed from Old French ache, from Vulgar Latin *acca. The source is unclear, but may descend from the vowelless alphabetic sequence ha ka 'H, K' (becoming [aka] when the [h] ceased to be pronounced), as K had low frequency in Late Latin. Doublet of ecchi.
examples: The word hour is written with a silent aitch.
The word length, which contains only four sounds l e ng th, is usually spell'd thus, el ee en gee tee aitch.
She frowned, hearing Lim Cheng Po's voice, so English, so refined, so very English upper-class. And often she had had to tell Joe about his aitches.

senses: To cut using a strimmer/string trimmer.
ety: Back-formation from strimmer, originally a trademark.
examples: Videos showed a badger entering a sett less than two metres from where the contractors had been using petrol hedge-trimmers to strim brambles, the resident said.

senses: A long jacket with a hood which protects the wearer against rain and wind.
ety: 1780, ultimately from Tundra Nenets парка (parka), via Aleut parka and Russian па́рка (párka). Perhaps from Proto-Uralic; see dialectal Finnish parka (“rag, swaddling clothes”), which may be a cognate from Proto-Uralic, or an early borrowing from another Uralic language.
examples: Basir tended to wear a beige suede parka over his shalwar kameez.

senses: An extraction or essence of something, obtained by boiling it down.
The process of boiling something down in this way.
ety: From Old French decoccion, decoction, from Latin decoctiō, from decoquō (“to boil down”), from de- + coquō (“to cook”).
examples: The transition is a keen one, I assure you, from a schoolmaster to a sailor, and requires a strong decoction of Seneca and the Stoics to enable you to grin and bear it.
Poley offered a hot decoction of blackberries, saying: Peace?
Witches and devils no longer threaten you and me. We don’t mind living next door to the harmless lady with her herb garden and decoction still, her black cat and red hair.

senses: Of hair or clothing, full-bodied or puffy; puffed out away from head or body.
ety: From French bouffant, from Middle French; present participle of bouffer (“to puff”). Doublet of buffont.
examples: Her bouffant suit made her seem much heavier than her petite figure actually was.

senses: An Italian grape-based spirit of between 80 and 100 proof, made from the distillation of pomace.
A variety or serving of grappa.
ety: Borrowed from Italian grappa. Doublet of grape.
examples: Wines, a few cocktails and grappas but no mixed drinks: 34 Downing Street (Bedford Street)

senses: Biological; pertaining to biology or to a living organism.
ety: From biology + -ic.
examples: Biologic femaleness is a sequence of circular returns, beginning and ending at the same point.
A biologic therapy that delays the onset of type 1 diabetes received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration on Thursday.

senses: To remove insects from (somewhere), especially lice.
ety: From de- + bug.
examples: You can debug yourself at home with various over-the-counter medications.
If you find nits, it's time for some serious debugging.
Before we moved into our new quarters we, and our belongings, had to be deloused and debugged.

senses: A vaccinationist; one who supports vaccination.
ety: From vax (“vaccine, vaccination”) + -er.
examples: Even among the very hesitant if the cost of vaccine denial is understood in human terms, uptake has been shown to be increased. Parents, vaxxers and anti-vaxxers alike, want the best for their children.

senses: Intentionally delaying (someone or something), intended to cause delay, gain time, or adjourn decision.
Slow or tardy.
ety: From Middle English dilatorie, from Old French dilatoire, from Latin dīlātōrius (“extending or putting off (time)”), from dīlātor, from differō. Not etymologically related to delay.
examples: Alva, as usual, brought his dilatory policy to bear upon his adversary with great effect.

senses: An object located between two or more things and hence separating them.
A device for removing one substance from another, such as cream from milk.
One who separates; an agent performing the action of separating.
ety: Borrowed from Latin sēparātor.
examples: When applying polish, always use toe separators to keep toes apart.
Death, the mystery, the great separator of friend from friend and loved one from loved one

senses: One who has received the highest of the four minor orders in the Catholic Church, being ordained to carry the wine, water and lights at Mass.
An altar server.
An attendant, assistant, or follower.
A devoted follower, fan, especially an overly eager one, following blindly.
ety: From Middle English acolite, acolit, from Old French acolyt and Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).
examples: The kneeling acolyte chimed a sacring-bell, and the congregation bent and swayed like a wheat-field swept scross by sudden wind.

senses: The position or state of being a son.
ety: From son + -ship.
examples: Jesus' unusual conception and birth were by no means the chief ways in which the first Christians expressed their sense of his divine sonship.

senses: A pike (type of fish).
ety: From pike + -y.
examples: In 1876, in twelve fishings in the same months, there were caught 31 Pikeys, 4 Spotted Dogs, and 441 Nowds.
A pikey's a pike. It's the dirtiest fish in the water.
The boated Pikey makes a series of tailstands as it lunges about, biting at feet, bags, hands, creels and thwarts.

senses: A zinc-coated steel one-cent (penny) coin, produced during World War II because of copper shortages.
A steel bearing ball used as a marble.
A steel wheel.
ety: From steel + -ie.
examples: The steelies were just balls of steel, industrially ugly and not part of most girls' collections. There were four sizes of marbles and we called them boulders, biggies, regulars, and teenies.

senses: The cry of a hen or goose, especially when laying an egg.
A laugh resembling the cry of a hen or goose.
Futile or excessively noisy talk.
A group of hyenas.
ety: From Middle English caclen, cakelen, perhaps from Old English *caclian, *cacolian, from Proto-West Germanic *kakulōn, *kakilōn (“to cackle, gaggle, yelp, snarl”), perhaps of imitative origin. By surface analysis, cack + -le. Compare Dutch kakelen (“to cackle”), German Low German kakeln (“to cackle”), German kakeln (“to blather”), Danish kagle (“to cackle”), Swedish kackla (“to cackle”). Compare also Old English cahhetan, ċeahhettan (“to laugh loudly; cackle”), German gackern (“to cackle”).
examples: I heard a grey hen cackling among the ling; I called and thought, "If I could get a sight of you now, it would be your last cackle;" just then I heard something moving behind me on the path.
There's no time to waste on silly cackle.
A cackle of hyenas might take on one male lion, but two is one too many.

senses: Any indigenous polytheistic religion.
Any of a class of religions often associated with nature rituals.
ety: From Latin pāgānismus (“heathenism”), from pāgānus (“peasant, rural, rustic”). The term was used pejoratively by local Orthodox Christian Demonyms to belittle what remained of alternative native ideas and ideals. By surface analysis, pagan + -ism.
examples: Most people in that region practise their own form of paganism.
Various neopagan movements have arisen, each advancing its own form of paganism. Some are monotheist.

senses: Someone who aspires (for high office, etc.)
ety: Borrowed from French aspirant.
examples: The company received dozens of applications from job aspirants.
Every aspirant actor dreams of making it to Broadway.
He was an aspirant to the presidency, though his chances were slim.

senses: A high-status courtesan in Japan.
ety: From Japanese 花魁, literally ‘flower-leader’.
examples: The oiran of Mitarai was not like the geisha. Like the great eighteenth-century courtesans of Europe, she knew who and what she was and turned wanton provocation into an art.

senses: Prim and fussy; too precise; overparticular.
Well-mannered; well-behaved.
ety: 1895, either an alteration of precise, blend of prim + sissy, or a blend of prim + fussy; first attested in a work of American writer Joel Chandler Harris.
examples: European languages like English are just prissier about getting that pronoun in there.
You drive like one of those prissy ladies at lunch who won't take the last cookie in case somebody else wants it.

senses: The process of falling asleep.
The death and assumption into heaven of the Virgin Mary.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French dormition, from Latin dormītiōnem.
examples: The Virgin had allegedly given away her robe just before her death – what is in Eastern tradition called her Dormition, or falling asleep.

senses: Chiefly preceded by in or on: the state each year during which a male animal (usually a camel or an elephant) exhibits increased aggressiveness and sexual activity due to a high level of testosterone.
An instance of this.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi मस्त (mast) / Urdu مَسْت (mast, “drunk, intoxicated; lustful”); and also from Middle Hindi مَسْت (mst /⁠mast⁠/)), and from its etymon Classical Persian مَسْت (mast, “(adjective) drunk, intoxicated; (literary) in rut; of an elephant: in musth; (noun) drunkard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to be wet; to become wet”).
examples: No animal in the world is so dangerous as an elephant in must.
I couldn't see the driver, and across my mind it rushed / That the Commissariat elephant had suddenly gone musth.
I have seen men deal with enraged elephants and live; but never was man yet born of woman that met my lord the elephant in his musth and lived to tell of the taming.

senses: Covered in spines or thorns.
Troublesome; difficult or vexing.
Like a spine in shape; slender.
ety: From spine + -y.
examples: The spiney desarts of scholastic philosophy

senses: The oil or perfume made from these plants.
ety: Borrowed from Tamil பச்சுளி (paccuḷi).
examples: Well she looks at you so coolly / And her eyes shine like the moon in the sea / She comes in incense and patchouli

senses: Petroleum jelly.
Any particular kind of petroleum jelly or of any similar lubricant.
ety: From German Wasser (“water”) + Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “oil”) + -ine. Genericized trademark of the Vaseline brand of petroleum jelly introduced by American chemist Robert Augustus Chesebrough in 1872.
examples: Hearts of putty, hearts of vaseline...

senses: Humbled; lowered, especially in rank, position, or prestige.
Synonym of abaissé.
ety: From abase + -ed.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:abased.
The blazon will be - A fess abased potentée of Champagne towards the point. The peculiar potent of Champagne may be seen in Bouton, Nouveau Traité de Blason, p. 199 (Paris, 1863.)

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a cat.
With subtle hostility in an effort to hurt, annoy, or upset (particularly in interactions between women).
ety: From cat + -y. Compare Dutch kattig, which also means “subtly hostile” and is formed the same way (kat + -ig); see also catfight.
examples: The fact is, Mr Carrados, Gertrude is a misfire. It was the surprise of her life (if I said "disappointment" you'd think me catty) when Mark married me, and she didn't set out to be pleasant to the interloper.

senses: The landlord (manager or owner) of a public house (“a bar or tavern, often also selling food and sometimes lodging; a pub”).
The manager or owner of a hotel.
ety: Probably from public house (“(Britain) bar or tavern, often also selling food and sometimes lodging, pub”) or public (“open to all members of a community”) + -an (suffix forming agent nouns), apparently originally used humorously.
examples: I went into a public-'ouse to get a pint o' beer, / The publican 'e up an 'sez, 'We serve no red-coats here.'

senses: located in the south, southern; later especially, often pertaining to the southern parts of Europe.
of or characteristic of southern areas or people, especially those in the southern parts of Europe
ety: Borrowed from Middle French meridional, from Latin merīdiōnālis, from merīdiēs (“noon; south”).
examples: For much of the 19th century what we now know as South America was called Meridional America

As soon as he heard the news of the trial and execution, he summed up the incident as a monument to Catholic intolerance, meridional superstition and judicial bigotry – and he decided to do something about it.

senses: A traditional savoury or sweet Jewish dish consisting of a baked pudding of pasta, potatoes, or rice, with vegetables, or raisins and spices.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish קוגל (kugl), from Middle High German kugel(e) (“ball”), referring to the roundish appearance of some puddings. Further etymology uncertain; see German Kugel for more.
examples: With the dipsy-doodle, the kit and caboodle / The truth is brutal, your grandma's kugel
Our mother wanted us and loved us dearly. Her chicken and fish, her stews, her meatloaves, her lasagna and kugels and everything else were flavorful in their own, unadulterated way.

senses: In formal debating, an argument that challenges a certain mindset or assumption made by the opposing team, often from the perspective of critical theory, rather than dealing directly with the topic under debate.
ety: Borrowed from German Kritik.
examples: Too much debate theory is based on power rather than reason. Kritiks are used as big sticks to avoid one of the duties closely associated with debating — research.
You can make most theory answers without cards, but some cards do exist which specifically criticize kritiks on a theoretical basis.
